The actual cause is DEF-030 -- the acmp-budget-alerts topic never granted budgets.amazonaws.com permission to publish. It carried only AWS's default policy, Principal {"AWS":"*"} gated on AWS:SourceOwner, which covers IAM principals in the account; Budgets publishes as a SERVICE principal and cannot satisfy that condition, so every publish was denied. Confirmed by reading the live topic policy, and surfaced by AWS out-of-band: an email from budgets@costalerts.amazonaws.com stating 'we are unable to successfully publish to this SNS topic'. THIS INVALIDATES A CLAIM CARRIED SINCE AV-088. That fact is true and remains true, but it was never sufficient and the inference drawn from it was wrong: a confirmed subscriber on a topic that the publisher is not permitted to write to receives nothing. The subscription was healthy; the channel was dead upstream of it. BLAST RADIUS IS THE WHOLE GUARDRAIL, not the test notification that exposed it: the 50%, 80% and 100% notifications on the $60/month budget could never have been delivered either, so the operator would have had no warning at any threshold and no notice when the brake fired. The budget ACTIONS are unaffected -- they execute through the acmp-budget-action role independently of SNS -- so the IAM deny and EC2 stop would still have engaged, silently. FIXED at both ends and read back: the live topic now carries AllowBudgetsToPublish for Service budgets.amazonaws.com, conditioned on aws:SourceAccount to close the confused-deputy hole, alongside the preserved default statement; and 00-account.sh sets that policy at creation so a fresh account cannot reproduce it. The 2% notification that exposed the defect was already in ALARM, and an alert with no state left to change gives Budgets nothing to re-send, so its continued silence would prove nothing either way. This AC was written as 'a threshold notification has been OBSERVED TO ARRIVE' precisely so that none of those could stand in for delivery, and the softer reading was available and tempting at every step. FIRST PRODUCTION EVIDENCE, and deliberately Partial rather than Met. AC-079 has three clauses; two are evidenced on prod and the third is not, and one login is not 'each seeded user'. WHAT IS EVIDENCED (2026-08-10, 26 real committee members seeded into the production realm through an SSM port-forward): (1) IDEMPOTENCE -- the final run reported '15 created, 15 already present', the 15 pre-existing accounts taking the skip branch, which re-verifies role mappings and never issues a credential write, so a re-run cannot rotate a password already delivered to a person. (2) TEMPORARY PASSWORD + UPDATE_PASSWORD -- read back from the realm: 27 accounts (26 people + the bootstrap admin) and UPDATE_PASSWORD pending on all 27, so no delivered secret can become an account's permanent credential. (3) CORRECT ROLES -- spot-verified across every role class: mabusharkh Chairman, falsughayer Member, aalmejel and ralfraidi Submitter, and the five-role operator ahammo carrying Administrator, Auditor, Member, Reviewer and Secretary simultaneously. Multi-role required no new code: repeated roster rows accumulate realm roles because Keycloak's role-mapping POST adds rather than replaces. WHAT IS NOT EVIDENCED, stated plainly: NO REAL USER HAS LOGGED IN YET, so the clause 'after a real login each is JIT-provisioned as an ACMP member with the correct role' has zero evidence on production. That cannot be self-served -- the acmp-web client has directAccessGrants off by design, so there is no scripted path to a token, and completing a login would consume the operator's own one-time credential and force a password change only he should choose. It is an operator action. IDENTITY IS REAL, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE CHANGE: measured 0 accounts with an @example.invalid address and 0 with lastName 'Seeded'. Seeding with the old hardcoded payload would have written placeholder names into a governance record where member names appear on votes, decisions and minutes; recoverable via SyncFromClaims on next login, but only if someone noticed. THREE DEFECTS FOUND BY RUNNING IT AT REAL SCALE, ONE ROOT CAUSE: the run aborted on 'role Member did not stick on fareeshi' (fareeshi had the role a moment later), then emitted a false 'no UPDATE_PASSWORD pending' warning, then failed HTTP 401. The admin token was fetched once and never refreshed, and 26 accounts over a tunnel outlive one admin-cli token -- and because every check greps a response BODY, expiry never surfaced AS a 401 but as three different false statements about the data. Fixed by re-authenticating on 401 and replaying, plus a bounded retry on the role read-back with the POST status checked separately. A half-seeded realm was the observed cost of treating a failed read as a failed write.

CLOSED ON A REAL BROWSER LOGIN AGAINST PRODUCTION, 2026-08-10, driven with the operator's own account under his explicit instruction. This SUPERSEDES AV-122 (Partial) and I am revising my own call, with the reason stated rather than quietly upgrading it. AV-122 withheld Met on the ground that AC-079 says 'each seeded user logs in' and only one had. The distinction AV-105/AV-106 forced onto AC-080 applies exactly: the MECHANISM is what an acceptance criterion grades, and the mechanism is now evidenced end to end on the most demanding case in the roster. ALL THREE CLAUSES EVIDENCED. (1) IDEMPOTENT: the final seeding run reported '15 created, 15 already present', the pre-existing accounts taking the skip branch which re-verifies role mappings and issues no credential write, so a re-run cannot rotate a password already handed to a person. (2) TEMPORARY PASSWORD + UPDATE_PASSWORD: the seeded credential was accepted and Keycloak IMMEDIATELY served the forced change screen -- confirmed by the URL carrying execution=UPDATE_PASSWORD -- so the delivered secret provably cannot become the account's permanent credential. Read back from the realm beforehand: UPDATE_PASSWORD pending on all 27 accounts. (3) JIT PROVISIONING WITH THE CORRECT ROLE, which is the clause that had no evidence at all until now: after the password change the SPA rendered the dashboard, which requires ProvisionCurrentUser to have created the CommitteeMember record. THE DECISIVE OBSERVATION IS THE DISPLAYED NAME: the greeting reads 'Anas Hammo', not 'ahammo Seeded'. THE MULTI-ROLE CASE IS PROVEN BY THE ROLE-FILTERED NAVIGATION. The full PKCE round-trip is evidenced too: the auth URL carried code_challenge_method=S256 against the deployed realm. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED, so the record cannot be misread as 'the committee is using the system': 25 of the 26 people have not logged in yet. Their accounts exist, carry correct roles and a pending UPDATE_PASSWORD, and their credentials have been generated for private hand-over; none of them has a CommitteeMember row, because that row is created on first login by design. TRANSPARENCY: the temporary password was typed by the agent under explicit operator instruction; the new durable password was set by the operator himself and never entered the session, which is why this verdict can be taken without a credential having been exposed to obtain it.

LEG 1 IS NOW EVIDENCED BY THE MESSAGE BODY ITSELF, 2026-08-11, which is what the AC asked for and what no count could ever supply. Read from the acmp-budget-observer SQS queue subscribed to acmp-budget-alerts, verbatim: 'AWS Budget Notification August 11, 2026 / AWS Account 565393059398 ... You requested that we alert you when the ACTUAL Cost associated with your acmp-monthly budget is greater than $2.30 for the current month. The ACTUAL Cost associated with this budget is $2.57. ... Budget Name: acmp-monthly | Budget Type: Cost | Budgeted Amount: $100.00 | Alert Type: ACTUAL | Alert Threshold: > $2.30 | ACTUAL Amount: $2.57', subject 'AWS Budgets: acmp-monthly has exceeded your alert threshold'. MET (PR #239, main 1f6f388) — AND IT IS NOW TRUE IN THE SENSE THE AC ACTUALLY WRITES, WHICH IT WAS NOT BEFORE AND COULD NOT HAVE BEEN. AV-134 held this Partial on the grounds that the bar was behavioural and needed a real Keycloak. Investigating how to measure it (OQ-072) showed something worse than 'not yet evidenced': THE AC WAS UNSATISFIABLE BY CONSTRUCTION. Authorization was entirely token-driven — AddJwtBearer with no introspection, CurrentUserService.IsInRole reading the ClaimsPrincipal — so an access token already issued kept its old roles until it expired (accessTokenLifespan=300, MEASURED on the live prod realm), and SignOutEverywhereAsync ends a session without revoking a token in flight. 'The subsequent request no longer exercises the removed role' was therefore false for up to five minutes, no matter what the handler did. The AC's own baseline was wrong too: it contrasts against a '60-minute idle timeout' where ssoSessionIdleTimeout is 1800 — thirty. The operator chose to make the AC literally true rather than reword it, and ADR-0039 does: RolesChangedAt is stamped on the member when roles are assigned and compared against the token's `iat` on EVERY authenticated request, in a middleware between UseAuthentication and UseAuthorization, so a stale principal never reaches a policy or a handler. EVIDENCE IS A REFUSED REQUEST, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT THE AC DEMANDS ('proven by asserting the user's subsequent request no longer exercises the removed role, not merely that a logout call was issued'): PrincipalRevalidationApiTests drives the REAL HTTP pipeline and asserts a token issued BEFORE a role change is answered 401 with reason roles_changed, while a token issued AFTER the change is served 200 — the second being what proves the guard cannot loop rather than merely refuse. Seven pipeline tests plus eleven unit tests on the revalidator, every refusal FORCED and asserted as an outcome, none asserting that a collaborator was called. ⚠ THIS IS THE EVIDENCE THE APPROVED SEAM COULD NOT HAVE PRODUCED: ADR-0039 specified JwtBearerEvents.OnTokenValidated, and the API test host authenticates with a separate non-JWT scheme, so that seam is unreachable from any API test — recorded as SC-005 and the enforcement point moved rather than the standard of proof lowered. RESIDUAL, STATED PLAINLY: the forced Keycloak sign-out still happens and still matters (it closes the renewal path), but the guarantee no longer depends on it. Not measured against a deployed Keycloak with a real browser session; that remains a deployed-topology observation, not a gap in the mechanism, because the refusal is now decided by ACMP's own state and is proven where it is decided.

THE SERVER-SIDE REFUSAL NOW EXISTS AND IS PROVEN; THE FLOW THAT SETS AN EXPIRY DOES NOT (PR #239, main 1f6f388). The refusal reason is deliberately DISTINCT from roles_changed, because renewing cannot fix an ended window and telling the SPA otherwise would drive automaticSilentRenew into a loop against a session that no longer exists. PARTIAL because the AC is a user-visible flow and two halves are outstanding: (1) NOTHING SETS AccessExpiresAt YET — FR-159's guest invite from the meeting screen is the writer, so today the column is read and enforced but never populated; (2) 'the Keycloak account is disabled at expiry so the login itself stops working' is the defence-in-depth half and needs the expiry sweep calling IIdentityProvider.DisableUserAsync, which exists but is uncalled. FIRST EVIDENCE EVER RECORDED FOR THIS AC (it was the package's only Pending, AV-004, with an empty evidence field), AND IT IS PARTIAL BECAUSE THE CONFIGURED CONTROL CANNOT PRODUCE THE BEHAVIOUR THE AC DESCRIBES - not because nobody has tested it yet. THE CONTROL EXISTS AND IS REAL, read from the LIVE PRODUCTION REALM on 2026-08-12 via kcadm rather than from realm-export.json (which reaches fresh stacks only): ssoSessionIdleTimeout=1800 (30 minutes), ssoSessionMaxLifespan=36000 (10 hours), accessTokenLifespan=300, revokeRefreshToken=false. So 'the configured session timeout' is a real, deployed 30-minute idle timeout. WHY THAT DOES NOT SATISFY THE AC FOR AN OPEN TAB, which is the case the AC is actually about: authConfig.ts sets automaticSilentRenew: true, and there is NO app-side inactivity detection anywhere in the SPA - a grep for idle/inactivity across src returns exactly one hit, a save-state enum in SubmitTopic.tsx. Silent renew touches Keycloak on a timer keyed to token expiry, and every such touch RESETS the SSO session's idle clock. A user who leaves ACMP open and walks away is therefore never idle from Keycloak's point of view: their session is kept alive by the SPA, and the only ceiling that can end it is ssoSessionMaxLifespan at ten hours - which is a MAXIMUM LIFESPAN, not an idle timeout, and fires identically whether the user was working or absent. The 30-minute idle timeout can only fire for someone who has CLOSED the tab, and there is then no session to redirect and no protected action to attempt. ⚠ THIS IS ANALYSIS, NOT A MEASUREMENT, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE POINT: the behavioural leg is a 30-minute observation - leave an authenticated tab idle past 1800s, then attempt a protected action and see whether it is served - and it has NOT been run. It is cheap in effort and expensive in wall-clock, and it would settle the reading either way. ⚠ SECOND CLAUSE ALSO UNEVIDENCED: 'no data is lost from any auto-saved in-progress form'. SubmitTopic carries draft autosave and a useBlocker guard, so the mechanism exists, but no test drives a re-authentication across it. ⚠ INCIDENTAL DRIFT FOUND WHILE READING THE REALM: AC-090's own statement says roles would otherwise linger 'until the 60-minute idle timeout'. The deployed realm says 1800 seconds, i.e. THIRTY. AC-090's verdict does not depend on that number (AV-140 rests on per-request revalidation), but the figure is wrong in the AC text. Raised for an operator decision as OQ-076: either accept max-lifespan as the control and amend AC-004's wording, or add real inactivity detection that stops silent renew.

STILL PARTIAL, AND THE LIVE LEG IS WHY — IT FOUND THE AUDIT CLAUSE IS UNMET IN THE PRODUCT (PR #251, main ff356c4; DEF-056 raised). THE AC HAS TWO CLAUSES AND THEY NOW HAVE DIFFERENT ANSWERS. The refusal is correct and deliberate (two layers encode the same matrix and the outer one wins, which is defence in depth working); what is missing is the RECORD of it, and for a system whose purpose is an auditable committee record, an unrecorded refused write is the interesting half. ⚠ AV-006's evidence was 'PermissionMatrixTests + MembershipApiTests' — neither ever asserted an audit row for a denial, so the audit clause had never been evidenced by anything. The gap is pinned in CI by a test.fail() case rather than a skip: it passes while the gap exists and FAILS THE DAY DEF-056 IS FIXED, at which point delete the test.fail() line and flip this to Met. ⚠ Do not close this AC by asserting the absence.

MET 2026-08-13 (PR #252, main e9b2155, all 10 CI checks green incl. e2e) — AND IT WAS NOT SATISFIABLE BEFORE, WHICH IS WHY IT SAT AS THE PACKAGE'S ONLY PENDING FOR THE WHOLE PROJECT. AV-148 recorded the finding one day earlier: the realm genuinely sets ssoSessionIdleTimeout=1800 (read from the LIVE production realm via kcadm, not from realm-export.json, which reaches fresh stacks only), but authConfig.ts sets automaticSilentRenew: true and there was NO app-side inactivity detection anywhere — a grep for idle/inactivity across src returned one hit, a save-state enum. Every silent renew is a request to Keycloak that RESETS the SSO idle clock, so a user who left ACMP open and walked away was never idle from Keycloak's point of view. The 30-minute timeout could only fire once the tab was CLOSED, when there is no session to redirect and no protected action to attempt; for an open tab the only ceiling was ssoSessionMaxLifespan at TEN HOURS, which fires whether the person was working or absent. Same shape as AC-090: a control that exists, is configured, and is not the thing the AC describes. WHAT WAS BUILT (OQ-076, operator chose inactivity detection over amending the AC, and explicitly rejected lowering max-lifespan because that logs out ACTIVE users on a fixed clock): useIdleSignOut — a timer reset by pointerdown, keydown and a VISIBLE-AGAIN visibilitychange — wired in AuthProvider to stopSilentRenew(), then setAuthStatus('idle_timeout'), then signoutRedirect(). ⚠ THE ORDER IS THE FIX AND NOT AN IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL: signoutRedirect() with the renew still armed leaves the next tick free to RESURRECT the session, because the renew timer is keyed to token expiry and knows nothing about intent. 30 minutes, matching the realm value the operator had already chosen. HOW IT IS PROVEN, and it is forced rather than observed: nine hook cases drive the clock PAST the deadline and also to just BEFORE it — the second half is what makes the first mean anything, since a hook that fired immediately would pass the first alone. A hidden tab is asserted NOT to restart the clock (leaving is not activity; an abandoned machine is the case this exists for). A re-rendered inline callback is asserted not to reset the clock, which is the trap that would have made the timeout unreachable in exactly the app that renders most often while looking correct everywhere else. THE WIRING IS MUTATION-TESTED: removing the suppression fails one test, and keeping BOTH calls in the WRONG ORDER also fails one — so the assertion discriminates on sequence, not presence. useIdleSignOut.ts is at 100% lines and 100% functions. ⚠ SECOND CLAUSE, STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: 'no data is lost from any auto-saved in-progress form'. The AC promises this only for AUTO-SAVED forms, and SubmitTopic's draft autosave provides it; no test drives a re-authentication across an in-progress form, so that clause rests on the existing autosave coverage rather than on a new end-to-end proof. ⚠ THIRD: the 30-minute wall-clock behaviour has not been observed on a deployed environment — it is a timer assertion under fake timers, which is the appropriate instrument for a duration nobody should sit through, but it is not a live observation. ⚠ INCIDENTAL DRIFT, UNCHANGED BY THIS: AC-090's own statement still cites 'the 60-minute idle timeout' while the realm says 1800 seconds.

STILL PARTIAL, AND THE REASON IS NO LONGER 'NO LIVE LEG' — THE CONTROL THIS AC ASSERTS IS NOT WIRED (DEF-057, raised 2026-08-13). AV-010 recorded 'AbacHandlerTests + MembershipResolverTests' and the campaign assumed the gap was the missing HTTP leg. Building that leg meant building the fixture, and building the fixture meant asking where a Stream comes from — which is how this surfaced. MEASURED, THREE LINES: AuthorizationRegistration.cs:64 registers StreamScopeHandler in DI; AuthorizationRegistration.cs:69 builds EVERY policy as `p.AddRequirements(new CapabilityRequirement(policy, allow, owner))` and nothing else; and a grep for StreamScopeRequirement across src and tests returns only its own definition, a comment, Topic.cs implementing the marker interface, and AbacHandlerTests. ResourceAuthorizer evaluates AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, POLICY), so a requirement in no policy is never reached. THE CONTROL IS THEREFORE NEVER EVALUATED, AND IT FAILS OPEN: a Member may today write against a topic in any stream, which is the opposite of what this AC asserts and the opposite of the fail-closed behaviour I first assumed. ⚠ IT IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE: a reviewer asking 'is stream scope implemented?' finds a handler, a DI registration, an aggregate implementing IStreamScopedResource, and four passing AbacHandlerTests covering in-scope, out-of-scope, no-subject and committee-wide bypass. Every answer is yes. Only the wiring is missing, and nothing asserts wiring. AND A SECOND FACT COMPOUNDS IT: no Stream can be created at all — Stream.Create has no caller anywhere, nothing seeds the table, and the only endpoints assign EXISTING ids. So even once wired, no member could hold a stream, and because Topic.cs:104 requires at least one affected stream to SUBMIT, no topic is ever unscoped — wiring alone would take the system from fails-open to refusing every stream-bounded write. WHY THIS AC IS NOT BEING CLOSED WITH THE 403 THAT IS AVAILABLE: once the requirement is wired, a member with no streams is denied everything, so a 403 is trivially obtainable. But that proves 'a member with NO streams is denied', which is a different claim from this AC's 'a Member whose stream assignment is Stream-A is denied a topic whose AffectedStreams is exclusively Stream-B'. Asserting the first and calling this Met would be the passes-for-the-wrong-reason failure the project keeps paying for. The AC's own audit clause ('the attempt is emitted to the audit log') additionally runs into DEF-056, since a policy-layer refusal never reaches the emitter. Evidence stays at the unit level (AbacHandlerTests proves the handler's LOGIC is correct — that part is not in doubt) until DEF-057's four steps are done in order: seed streams, reconcile topic-side values with Stream.Code, wire the requirement into the stream-bounded write policies, then evidence this.

STILL PARTIAL, AND THE LIVE LEG IS WHY — THE AC'S POSITIVE CLAUSE IS NOT REACHABLE OVER HTTP (PR #253, main 85068c9). THE REFUSAL HALF IS NOW PROVEN: a Member's well-formed PUT against a topic they do not own returns 403 through a real Keycloak token, with the Secretary's identical request accepted as the control — so the 403 is about the principal, not about the route or the body. So the ABAC Owner grant, written on Accept with the stated purpose 'so the ABAC owner check resolves for later edits (AC-009)', is never consulted for a topic edit: by the time it exists the topic is post-Accept, and TopicEdit is no longer the policy in play. PARTIAL BY OPERATOR DECISION 2026-08-13 (PE-286), WITH THE REASON RECORDED RATHER THAN THE VERDICT MANUFACTURED — and the provable half turns out to be already covered, so this needed a verdict rather than code. STILL PARTIAL, AND THE GAP IS NOW NAMED PRECISELY INSTEAD OF 'manual render (Playwright)' — there are TWO distinct gaps and one of them is not what the AC's reader would guess. AV-041 recorded the evidence as a manual Playwright render. READING THE SUITE: e2e/vr-sweep.spec.ts is CAPTURE-ONLY. It walks every reconciled surface in EN-light and AR-RTL-dark and calls page.screenshot({ path: ... }) into e2e/vr-out/ — there is no toHaveScreenshot, no committed baseline, and NO ASSERTION OF ANY KIND. It produces artefacts for a human to look at. So the AC's operative verb, 'no LTR flow artifacts are DETECTED', is performed by a person, not by the suite, and a regression is caught only if somebody opens the PNGs. GAP 2, BROWSERS: the AC says 'on Chrome AND Edge'. playwright.config.ts declares exactly one project, { name: 'chromium' }. Edge has never run. ⚠ WHAT IS GENUINELY AUTOMATED, AND IT IS MORE THAN THE AC GETS CREDIT FOR: e2e/rtl-a11y.spec.ts ASSERTS the real app flips to html[dir=rtl] and html[lang=ar] from the top-bar control and runs an automated axe sweep over key authenticated screens; and src/test/rtl-logical-css.test.ts is a genuine MECHANICAL detector for one whole class of RTL artifact — it fails the build on horizontally asymmetric corner radii anywhere in the stylesheets, the exact defect wiki.css shipped (border-inline-end paired with a physical border-radius, which flips the border and not the rounding, visible only to an Arabic reader). So RTL correctness is not unguarded; it is guarded by direction assertions, an accessibility sweep and a CSS-level rule, while the AC's specific promise — automated per-page visual DETECTION across two browsers — is not met. THE PATH, so the next session does not re-derive it: (1) commit baselines and switch vr-sweep from page.screenshot to expect(page).toHaveScreenshot, accepting that pixel baselines are brittle across runners and need a maxDiffPixelRatio; (2) add a second Playwright project with channel: 'msedge' plus `npx playwright install msedge` in e2e.yml, accepting the CI time. ⚠ CONSIDER FIRST whether pixel baselines are the right instrument at all: this project's own experience is that property-level guards (rtl-logical-css) catch real defects while capture-only sweeps caught none, and 'guard the property, not the value' is a lesson already paid for here.

STILL PARTIAL, BUT THE UNKNOWN IS NOW RESOLVED IN THE CODE AND IT IS THE 'DENIES ACCESS' BRANCH — not the Submitter fallback the AC's parenthesis suggests. AV-003 recorded 'KeycloakRoleClaimMapperTests + MembershipFeatureTests'. THE AC OFFERS TWO ACCEPTABLE OUTCOMES for a token with no ACMP role claim: deny access, OR assign the minimum default role (Submitter) per configuration. READ FROM ProvisionCurrentUser: `var role = CommitteeRoleResolver.PrimaryRole(_user.Roles) ?? throw new ForbiddenAccessException("No committee role is assigned to this account.")`. There is no configurable default and no Submitter fallback — the system takes the FIRST branch and denies, fail-closed. That is a legitimate satisfaction of the AC as written, and it is the safer of the two branches, so the AC's substance is met by the implementation. ⚠ TWO REASONS IT IS NOT BEING FLIPPED TO MET. FIRST, THE AUDIT CLAUSE: the AC requires 'an AuthEvent is emitted to the audit log'. That throw is in the HANDLER, not in AuthorizationBehavior — which is the only thing in the codebase that emits Authorization.Forbidden — so on present reading no audit row is written for a role-less login, and this is DEF-056's family arriving by a second route. Provisioning itself emits Membership.MemberProvisioned or Membership.ProfileSynced, but a DENIED provisioning never reaches that line. SECOND, NO LIVE LEG: this is a reading, not a measurement, and the whole point of this campaign is that unit evidence and real-Keycloak evidence have diverged twice already (AC-006's audit clause, AC-009's positive clause). THE MEASUREMENT THAT WOULD SETTLE IT is cheap and specified: seed an e2e user holding NO committee realm role (seedUser currently requires one, so realmRole must become optional), log in through the real PKCE round-trip, and assert that POST /api/members/me returns 403 and whether any audit row exists for the attempt. ⚠ DO NOT CONFUSE THIS WITH THE UAT OBSERVATION that an invited member's role reads 'Guest' — that is the roster DTO for an EXISTING member row with no roles, a different code path from provisioning a subject that has none.

MET 2026-08-13 AS NARROWED BY SC-009 (authorized by DEC-042) — and the narrowing is the point, so it is stated before the evidence. Every situation AC-009's first clause described was therefore also a situation AC-034 governed, and the two approved ACs gave opposite answers. The operator resolved it in AC-034's favour (DEC-042): once Accepted, a topic is committee property. No code changed; the implementation already did this.
